newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees "spy in sky" fish satellite system.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees "spy in sky" fish satellite system.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers struck a political agreement on Thursday to set up a satellite system to track vessels and curb illegal fishing, EU officials said.

The new system, which will start up in mid-1998, will allow fisheries protection agencies to monitor the identity, position and activities of vessels and will also improve fishing safety by allowing fast transmission and pinpointing of distress calls.
"(It's) a very strategic and significant tool in the ongoing battle against illegal fishing," said Irish Marine Minister Sean Barrett, who chaired the EU meeting.
"It's not a major milestone in fisheries control," Barrie Deas, chief executive of Britain's National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations, told Reuters.
Satellites only show where vessels are, not what they are doing, he added.
But the Irish Fishermen's Association's Frank Doyle said satellites were more efficient and cost-effective than building fisheries protection vessels.
Agreement was achieved quickly after Italy lifted its objections, an EU official said, adding that a formal legal text would be adopted early in 1997.
Italy's change of mind meant that opposition from Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands and Sweden could be overridden under the EU's weighted voting system.

Italy came on board after receiving a pledge of 100 million Ecus of EU aid for a three-year scheme starting in mid-1997 for Italian driftnet fishermen hunting swordfish in the Mediterranean to switch to other activities, officials said.

Satellites will start to track fishing vessels in certain areas from June 30, 1998 and the system will become fully operational from January 1, 2000, when all vessels over a total length of 24 metres, fishing more than 12 miles offshore and for longer than 24 hours will be tracked.
Satellites will transmit information back to the home countries which will then pass it on to the country in whose waters the boats were fishing.
Capital investment costs will be covered from a 205-million- Ecu ($254 million), five-year EU fisheries control fund.
Spain, which has the biggest fishing fleet, will be the most affected with 1,000 large, distant-water vessels subject to satellite controls, or 25 percent of the total.
Italy would have 800 vessels tracked and the Dutch 350.
